blocks.text: 1. Indexing

blocks.alt: Raw vectors go through an index to enable fast search

blocks.text: What Is A Vector Database defined the storage layer. Indexing covers how a vector database organizes vectors for fast search, moving from raw storage to actual searchability.
It builds an internal structure that avoids checking every single stored vector one by one.
2. The Raw Storage Alone
Storing vectors without any organization still forces brute force comparison at search time.
Storage alone does not solve the speed problem introduced in this module's first topic.
3. What An Index Actually Does

blocks.alt: All vectors are compared against an indexed search path

blocks.text: An index is a precomputed structure that narrows the search space before comparing vectors directly.
It dramatically reduces how many vectors actually need to be checked per query.
4. Indexing As A Preprocessing Step
Building the index happens once, up front, before any queries ever arrive.
That upfront cost gets paid back many times over across every future query.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Phase","When it happens"],"rows":[["Index building","Once, before any queries arrive"],["Query search","Repeatedly, using the already built index"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Approximate Nearest Neighbor Preview

blocks.alt: A query goes through an ANN index to produce approximate neighbors

blocks.text: As with approximate not exact search in What Is A Vector Database, most indexes trade a small accuracy loss for a large speed gain.
Those specific indexing algorithms get their own full treatment in the next module.
6. Index Build Time Versus Query Time

blocks.alt: Build time is slow and happens once while query time is fast and repeated

blocks.text: A richer, more thorough index takes longer to build but answers queries faster.
That core tradeoff shapes almost every indexing decision a pipeline makes.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A pipeline willing to spend extra minutes building a more thorough index often earns back that time many times over through faster query responses across millions of future searches.

blocks.text: 7. Rebuilding After Large Changes

blocks.alt: Many updates trigger rebuilding the index

blocks.text: As with incremental ingestion in Document Ingestion, adding many new vectors at once can degrade an existing index's structure.
Periodic rebuilding keeps the index performing at its best over time.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: An index built once and never rebuilt can gradually lose search quality as large volumes of new vectors accumulate outside its original optimized structure, especially after major content additions.

blocks.text: 8. Index Parameter Tuning

blocks.alt: Speed is traded off against accuracy

blocks.text: Most indexes expose tunable parameters that trade accuracy against speed directly.
Adjusting those parameters lets a pipeline dial in its own preferred balance.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Parameter direction","Effect"],"rows":[["Favoring accuracy","Slower queries, results closer to the true nearest neighbor"],["Favoring speed","Faster queries, slightly less precise results"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Indexing As The Foundation For Everything Else

blocks.alt: Every vector query relies on indexing

blocks.text: Every later topic in this module, including collections, filtering, and sharding, builds on top of an already indexed vector store.
That makes indexing the structural foundation the rest of this module assumes.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates how a simple bucketing index narrows the search space compared to brute force.

code.content:
import random

def generate_fake_vectors(count, dimensions):
    return [[random.random() for _ in range(dimensions)] for _ in range(count)]

def simple_bucket_index(vectors, num_buckets):
    # what an index actually does
    buckets = {i: [] for i in range(num_buckets)}
    for idx, v in enumerate(vectors):
        bucket_id = int(v[0] * num_buckets) % num_buckets
        buckets[bucket_id].append(idx)
    return buckets

vectors = generate_fake_vectors(10_000, dimensions=32)
index = simple_bucket_index(vectors, num_buckets=20)

query = generate_fake_vectors(1, dimensions=32)[0]
query_bucket = int(query[0] * 20) % 20
candidates_in_bucket = index[query_bucket]

print(f"Total vectors in collection (the raw storage alone): {len(vectors):,}")
print(f"Candidates checked using the index: {len(candidates_in_bucket):,}")
print(f"Reduction: only checking about {len(candidates_in_bucket) / len(vectors) * 100:.1f}% of the full collection")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the index narrowing the search down to a small fraction of the full collection, instead of checking every single stored vector.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Storing vectors without building any index and relying on brute force search at scale.
Never rebuilding an index after large volumes of new vectors have accumulated.
Tuning index parameters purely for accuracy without considering the resulting query latency.
Assuming index build time is wasted effort rather than an investment repaid across future queries.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Indexing builds an internal structure that avoids checking every single stored vector per query.
Raw storage alone still forces brute force comparison, which an index is built to avoid.
An index is a precomputed structure that narrows the search space before direct comparison.
Index building happens once, up front, and pays off across every future query.
Most indexes trade a small accuracy loss for a large speed gain, covered in depth in the next module.
A richer index takes longer to build but answers queries faster, a core tradeoff to manage.
Large volumes of new vectors can degrade an index, requiring periodic rebuilding.
Tunable index parameters let a pipeline dial in its own preferred accuracy versus speed balance.
